column2: Snapshots go out 30 times a second: on every tick at 30 Hz, and on every second tick in the 60 Hz margin run (R2-BUD-REC1's snapshot half, below); inputs are sampled and sent every tick.
It does so in the client endpoint, ADR 0002's `client-endpoint` crate (no bindings, transport or clock), which the native headless test clients run too.

On every snapshot it resets the local player (and its vehicle) to the server's state for the last command the server ran and replays the newer commands through the same Rust code (Quake III's method), in ADR 0004 part 3's prediction step (only the prediction scope's phases, for the local slot and its vehicle, against the static world and the movers as last decoded, drawing from no random stream); it skips the replay when the server's state matches the stored prediction.

A replay emits no event its first run already emitted: the player's own cues are keyed by (entity, weapon, command sequence), so a replayed shot plays its muzzle flash and sound once ("Cues are events keyed by (entity, ability or weapon, command sequence)": r1-simulation-core.md, Recommendations, unit abilities, R1-ABL-REC4, lines 2427–2428), and the server never sends a client its own cosmetic shot events (part 6).

The replay covers 200 ms of game time (6 ticks at 30 Hz) within 1 ms p99 on the minimum laptop (R1-TICK-REC2 P3); its real depth is the round trip plus the input buffer plus one tick, 5 to 7 ticks at P2 with a 1–3 tick buffer ((100 + 33.3 + 33.3) ÷ 33.3 to (100 + 100 + 33.3) ÷ 33.3, arithmetic) and deeper at P3 and P4, so the proof test records the depth per profile.

The snapshot's own-state section carries everything the replay reads for the local soldier and its vehicle: position and velocity, its weapon state, and the active effect rows (or the attribute values they produce) that own movement and own weapon state read, upgrade picks and ability effects included (ADR 0005 leaves how the predicting sim gets them to this record), so a pick or an effect that changes move speed or a fire interval causes no correction; that section is sent unquantised, or the server quantises its own copy the same way each tick, and like every field it is sent when it changes (its real size is measured, R2-XU-OQ15).
Never predicted: damage, deaths and hits on others; the uplink countdown and steals; purchases; upgrade offers and picks; weapon pickups (interim:

The repeats are delta-coded against the newer command beside them: option U2, which R2-BUD-REC1 takes up "once measured" (r2-netcode.md, Recommendations, Brief question 2, lines 2302–2303), adopted from the start because this command, with its aim point, is about twice R2's 8 B input, and sent whole at the cap it would break the upstream mark (the bandwidth estimate); the proof test measures both forms (R2-XU-OQ4).

Each snapshot acknowledges two commands: the newest one the server received, which ends its repeats, and the last one it ran, the state the client's replay starts from (part 4); with only the second, the repeats would also span the input buffer's 1–3 ticks.

The server checks every command (every limit is data): its tick is not too far ahead of the server's and strictly newer than the last command run, so a client whose clock runs fast never runs more commands than the server has ticked plus that lead bound (equal ticks would let it run the per-tick cap on every tick: the security review, 2026-11-02); sequence numbers only move forward, wrap-around handled; the move vector's length is at most 1; a press counter advances by at most one edge per button for each tick the command covers; the aim point lies inside the map bounds (a point beyond the weapon's reach is clamped, not refused: below); fire, ability and reload edges meet the server's own cooldown, ammunition and reload state; the acknowledged snapshot is one the server sent; a datagram with trailing bytes or unknown fields is dropped whole; the commands it runs per client per tick are capped, the catch-up cap no larger than the redundancy cap (the lag-switch guard).

*Time:* the client estimates server time from its own ping samples (the browsers' `getStats()` is missing on Chrome and Edge and throws on Firefox), drifting at most 1–2 ms per frame, halving errors over 100 ms and resetting over 500 ms (Quake III's rules).

Every sample, and every jitter sample of part 7, is timed by its datagram's arrival: the Worker's host passes in, with each tick's input call, every datagram received since the last tick with the time it arrived, the time it sent the previous step's datagrams and its current time, all as plain values (ADR 0002 part 5), since timing a datagram at the tick that reads it would add up to one tick period (33.3 ms) of false jitter.
The client endpoint reads no clock itself (std's clock panics on the browser's Wasm target: the Rust review of 2026-11-02, reading std's source).

The server answers pings on its I/O runtime as they arrive; the client answers the server's at its next tick, and its pong carries the hold time, from the ping's arrival to the host's time at that step, which the server subtracts, at most one tick period's worth (a client that misreports it can only shrink its own RTT, or inflate it as part 8's accepted latency faking already allows).
The server keeps a per-client input buffer of 1–3 ticks (proposed), adapted per client; each command is stamped with the server tick it is meant for.

*The aim point:* the page posts its newest input once per drawn frame, with its cursor ray from the camera and the view time of the frame it drew (ADR 0002 part 5), and each tick the Worker builds the one network command from the newest post (running press totals, so a superseded post loses no press); it casts that ray with the sim crate's ray query (ADR 0004) against the static world and the interpolated remote entities it published for that view time, and quantises the hit point into the network command.

The server rebuilds the ray from its own fire origin at the command's tick (the `playerFireOrigin` rule, GC5) toward that point, extends it to or cuts it at the weapon's range and resolves it with part 8.

A point beyond the weapon's reach is clamped, never refused: a top-down cursor names points about 28 m from the look point, 44 m with the ADS pan (r2-netcode.md, Findings, R2-INT-F18, lines 847–851), against legacy's Beam Katana range of 3.6 m and Molotov range of 0 (LEGACY_TUNING.md:181), and a clamped point gives a cheat nothing, since the server builds the ray from its own origin.
Throws and charged shots take their heading and pitch from the same point; a melee swing and a throw stop at their own reach, and what a throw aimed past it does is rule data (ADR 0005).

*Research:* R2-SYNC-REC2 (changed: an aim point beyond reach is clamped, a command's tick must be strictly newer), R2-SYNC-REC8, R2-BUD-REC4 (the input buffer and the clock), R2-BUD-REC1 (changed: redundancy as R2-SYNC-REC2, the repeats delta-coded as its U2), R2-XU-OQ4, R1-XT-OQ1 = R2-XT-OQ1 = R4-XT-OQ1, R1-XT-OQ5 = R2-XT-OQ5, R1-TICK-OQ4, R1-TICK-OQ8;

A desync of client-side flight against the server is a defect of that function (ADR 0004's PM-0004-73 holds it bit-identical on every target), fixed there, not a reason to change the encoding: whole, E3b (projectiles in every snapshot) cannot pass the budgets (about 188.3 kbps at N = 48 in R2's estimate, above the 160 kbps mean: r2-netcode.md line 1779; in the stress scene 300 live projectiles × 5.5 B = 1,650 B per snapshot, above the 1,067 B cap before any soldier: arithmetic on line 1755), so it is kept only per projectile kind: a kind whose flight still desyncs rides in every snapshot, its live count × 5.5 B shown against the cap.
The server forces a resync when a client's event queue overflows (below); a client that has lost its state (a Worker restart, a long hidden tab) asks for one with `Resync` (message catalogue).

*Events:* tick-stamped gameplay events (the gameplay events of ADR 0004 part 19: hits, deaths and kills, purchases, uplink cache events, harvester deliveries and kills, structure kills and stage changes, tech tiers, upgrade picks and pickups) ride in the snapshot's event section, filtered per client by visibility class (part 9 (e); which economy events are team-private is R2-INT-OQ3), and are resent until the client's acknowledgement covers them; the per-client queue of unacknowledged events is bounded (data), and on overflow the server forces a full resync of that client or disconnects it.
Cosmetic events (shots, muzzle flashes, sounds) go once, and never to the client whose own shots they are (part 4).

Blasts are not cosmetic, since a lost one would hide an explosion: a blast that ends a projectile is that projectile's final trajectory change (its explosion, with tick and position), which the delta coding repeats until the client acknowledges it, so it needs no event of its own; any other blast (a vehicle's or a structure's) is a gameplay event, resent like one; beyond a projectile's relevance its blast reaches a client only as a cosmetic sound event inside part 9 (f)'s sound radius.
When each event plays is part 7's rule.
Vehicles carry hull and turret transforms and health per part; parts, and the pilot, travel with their parent.

*Wire widths:* entities are named by the sim's own id (kind, index, generation; never a library id); a record names kind and index, and the generation travels in the record that brings the entity into a client's set; a generation change at an index the client holds (a respawn in the same slot, ADR 0004 part 18) is sent as a removal plus an addition, which also tells the client to place that soldier, not slide it (part 7).
**Interpolation and the clock.** Remote entities are drawn at the delayed time, "server time minus the interpolation delay", from a snapshot buffer kept in the Worker.

Server time here is the client's own reading: the newest snapshot's server tick, advanced by the local clock since that snapshot arrived (its arrival stamp, part 5), so the delayed time trails the server's present by the downlink's one-way delay plus the interpolation delay.

The Worker publishes already-delayed remote poses in each per-tick block, and the page interpolates between the two newest blocks (R1-TICK-REC5, ADR 0004; drawing, ADR 0003), so what the page draws trails the newest block by up to one tick; that fraction is inside the view time the page reports (part 5).

The delay starts at 3 snapshot intervals (100 ms at 30 Hz), widens with jitter measured from the arrival stamps and narrows slowly on a clean link, within 2 to 5 intervals (66.7 to 166.7 ms at 30 Hz), as data.

*Events* follow the timeline of what they belong to: the Worker writes each spatial event (a remote soldier's action start or cosmetic shot, a hit on or the death of a remote entity, a blast, a structure kill) into the first block whose delayed time reaches the event's tick, so it plays with the drawn poses it belongs to ("Blasts are server events with a tick, played on the timeline of the entity they hit": r2-netcode.md, R2-SYNC-REC6, line 2210); the local player's own and predicted events, owner events (offers, pick and purchase results, the shooter's hit confirmation) and events tied to no entity on the delayed timeline (tech tiers, the uplink countdown) go into the next block at once, online and in a local match alike, since both run the client endpoint.

*Why:* three intervals is Fiedler's measured rule for 2–5 % loss, and with the buffer in the Worker the view time, the aim ray and the command are built in one place; an event played on arrival would run one interpolation delay ahead of its entity, so a remote death would start 0.9–1.5 m from the drawn soldier at 9 m/s (100–166.7 ms × 9 m/s, arithmetic).

*Research:* R2-SYNC-REC4 (changed: the buffer's side, one bound), R2-BUD-REC4 (changed), R2-SYNC-REC6 (its blast rule), R2-XU-OQ3, R1-XT-OQ3 = R2-XT-OQ2 = R3-XT-OQ1 = R5-XT-OQ2, R2-SYNC-OQ12 = R2-BUD-OQ7.
*Need:* VISION_V2 §4; §6.4 (big vehicles drawn smoothly); §6.8 (events stamped with ticks).
The view time is accepted if it lies within a tolerance of the server's own estimate, the tolerance at most one snapshot interval (33.3 ms at 30 Hz, data); otherwise the estimate is used.

The estimate is R2's "RTT plus that client's interpolation delay" (r2-netcode.md, R2-SYNC-REC5, lines 2145–2146), which is Source's model, where a command runs on arrival, plus the two waits that model has not got: the time this command waited in the server's input buffer (part 5), which the server knows, and half a tick for the page's blend of two blocks (part 7:
0 to 1 tick, so half a tick centres the estimate; proposed).
Neither holds against a cheat: a client can delay its replies (r2-netcode.md, lines 2150–2152) or, outside a browser, its QUIC acknowledgements, and so claim rewind up to the cap, an accepted risk.
The cap bounds the final rewind on every path: data, its value OQ-0001-5; beyond it, shooters lead by the excess.

For cheat detection later (detection is the security baseline's, ADR 0006), the server records each player's view-time offset and aim per command, and each client's quinn `rtt()` beside its own ping RTT once a second (proposed: a gap between the two is a detection signal), as raw entries in a per-match side file written beside the match record, keyed by slot and never by guest id, never in the `tracing` log stream:

48 × 30 = 1,440 entries a second, 1,728,000 in a 20-minute match (LOOP_V2 §8), about 518 MB as log lines at A-9's 300 B against its 200 lines a match (r6-infrastructure.md, lines 568–569) and about 27.6 MB at 16 B a raw entry (a slot, a tick, a view-time offset and a two-axis aim point:
ADR 0006 part 9's scale figure; arithmetic).
Raw entries, not per-player summaries (proposed: until the detection policy, item B7 of ADR 0006, says what it needs, nothing is summarised away);
ADR 0006 part 9 uploads the file with the record and keeps it 14 days.

On the round-trip reading of R2's profiles, a P2 player with a 100–150 ms delay needs a rewind of 200–250 ms by R2's formula (R2-SYNC-REC5's arithmetic), and 233–383 ms once the buffer (33.3–100 ms at 1–3 ticks) and the blend (0–33.3 ms) are added (arithmetic), so a 200 ms cap clips every honest shot at the latency VISION_V2 §4 names, and a 250 ms cap all but those with the shortest buffer and blend; the proof test records each shot's RTT, delay, buffer wait and blend, and the share each candidate cap clips (OQ-0001-5).

*Research:* R2-SYNC-REC5 (changed: the estimate adds the buffer wait and the blend), R2-BUD-REC4 (changed: history and cap follow R2-SYNC-REC5), R2-XU-OQ1, R2-XU-OQ2, R2-XU-OQ7, R2-SYNC-OQ2, R2-SYNC-OQ8, R2-SYNC-OQ9, R2-SYNC-OQ15.

(f) Events have a radius per event type (data; sound larger than visuals) and pass the area test; shots at or hitting the viewer are always sent; an event whose shooter is not relevant to the viewer carries no shooter id, and its origin is clipped to where the shot enters the viewer's region; big units are relevant by their bounds plus a per-type visual radius; parts, and the pilot, travel with their parent.

*Ports:* the port plan is OQ-0006-16 (infra-engineer with netcode-architect, confirmed by the Advisor); until it is answered, each room process listens on one UDP port for WebTransport and one TCP port for the WebSocket fallback, taken from the VM's two firewall ranges (ADR 0006 part 5; that question's option (a)), and the lobby hands the client the host and both ports (one process per room gives one port per room: r2-netcode.md, Findings, R2-ROOM-F18, line 1562); whether the fallback must also answer on TCP 443 is the same question's.

`Join` within 2 s, counted from the TCP accept or the QUIC handshake's first packet, so TLS and the WebSocket upgrade fall inside it (until then one stream, datagrams dropped), and a cap on handshakes in progress; a modest cap on connections per address (above 1), where an address is an IPv4 /32 or an IPv6 /64 (the prefix length is data: an IPv6 interface id is 64 bits, so one subnet gives a client 2^64 addresses:

RFC 4291 §2.5.1, read by the security review on 2026-11-02, not in the research), and every per-address limit of parts 10 and 11 keys the same way; new sessions rate-limited, with quinn's retry or refusal under load and `H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD` for abusers; an Origin allow-list answered with 403 on both transports;

Certificates are ADR 0006's: in production [a certificate per hostname](../research/GLOSSARY.md#game-server-certificate) (R6-HOST-REC4; carry-forward 4); development servers and the netcode proof test use self-signed, pinned certificates for WebTransport, valid at most 14 days, whose hash the page fetches from its own HTTPS origin (R2-TRN-REC5); whether the staging server that multiplayer previews use presents such a pinned certificate or the browser-trusted one on both transports (a hash written into a static preview goes stale) is OQ-0006-5's, with ADR 0002 part 10's two shapes; the WebSocket fallback cannot pin a hash, since its constructor takes only a URL and sub-protocols (r2-netcode.md, Findings, R2-ROOM-F12, lines 1494–1500), and presents the certificate ADR 0006's OQ-0006-5 names for development and staging.

**Rooms, the lobby and bots.** A room lives through Created → Open → Countdown → Running → Ended → Closed, with a timeout in each state (activation, an empty room, the mode's match length) and a health check for the supervisor.

`room` reads no clock and no OS randomness, since it also runs as the local server in the browser's Worker, where std's clock panics (the Rust review of 2026-11-02, reading std's source): its timers count ticks, their lengths in data (the state timeouts and the reconnect grace window, 60 s = 1,800 ticks at 30 Hz), while the `server` crate keeps the wall-time ones on its I/O side (the `Join` deadline and the handshake cap, per-connection and per-address rate limits, the ping schedule; part 10), and the host passes time in as a value.

A match never pauses or restarts for one player, and every match starts from a new sim instance, which also resets every player record, upgrade tracks included (UPGRADE-SCOPE; the record is ADR 0004's).

The tick thread and the I/O runtime share only bounded channels, never a lock the tick unwraps (a connection that panics while holding a lock would poison it for the tick: std's `Mutex`, the Rust review).

A panic on the tick thread is fatal to the room: the loop catches it at its top (`catch_unwind`), reports it (ADR 0006 part 10), sends `RoomEnded` with a crash reason where it can, marks the match record as crashed and exits the process non-zero, so the supervisor records the exit and the VM's other rooms go on; under `unwind` an uncaught panic "ends only its own thread" (r2-netcode.md, Findings, R2-ROOM-F8, lines 1459–1462) and would leave a room that holds its connections and sends nothing (ADR 0004 part 20 says the same; whether a match should ever resume instead is OQ-0001-18).

The lobby validates display names, and the room re-checks the length before the roster: bounds as data (a length in bytes and in code points), no Unicode control or format characters (categories Cc and Cf), NFC (proposed; the security review's).

The signature follows the security review's answer to R2-ROOM-OQ2: an asymmetric signature (the lobby signs; rooms hold only the public key), one pinned algorithm, an explicit token type and a key id for rotation, and a separate signing key per environment, each with its own key id, so staging rooms take only staging-key tokens and a production room refuses every staging or preview token whatever its Origin (ADR 0006 part 4 and item B5), the signature verified before the replay cache is touched, a bounded cache that refuses new tokens when full, and the room re-checking any pre-assigned team or slot against the mode; key storage waits on the security baseline (ADR 0006).

*Reconnect:* slot, team and squad are held for a grace window (data, proposed 60 s); the client fetches a fresh token; the newest connection for a player id wins and the older one is closed; whether a player who returns after the window gets their record (tracks, money) back is ADR 0004's OQ-0004-10 (GD-REJOIN:
Mustafa's, with OQ-0005-AB10; the record is ADR 0004's).

*Private rooms:* a short code that only locates the room, from a secure random source, with lookups limited per client, per address and globally and guest creation limited per address (addresses keyed as in part 10); the creator is the host, and the room checks every host command (start, kick, lock, team and faction settings) against the host's player id (whether a kick also bars that player for the rest of the match is OQ-0001-17); settings are fixed at start and carry a faction per team (VISION_V2 §3 [DECIDED]).
*Guests:* the lobby issues a guest id and a secret of at least 64 bits in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie (where the secret finally lives is R2-ROOM-OQ11, ADR 0006's);

SameSite=Strict sends it only with requests from the site that set it, a site being the registrable domain (MDN, Set-Cookie and Glossary "Site", read by the security review on 2026-11-02), so the client host and the lobby sit on one registrable domain (ADR 0006 part 6 and item B4; the domain is OQ-0006-15); the room only ever sees the join token.

Where the lobby and supervisor run, the room directory and the guest store are ADR 0006's; the directory records each room's build, protocol version and content hash, so the lobby can send a client only to rooms that match it (needed if releases run live, harmless in a release window: how releases reach running rooms is OQ-0006-14); the lobby asks a VM's supervisor for a new room and learns its host and ports (message catalogue; the link is ADR 0006 part 6's).

**In-match upgrades, purchases, weapon drops and pickups (UPGRADE-SCOPE, the network side).** The server is the authority over every player's upgrade tracks, the offers, the picks, the purchases, the weapon drops and the world pickups.
Offers (three choices by default; the offer's size is data, ADR 0005 AB-8) reach only their owner (owner class), in the owner's section of the snapshot, each with an offer id.

A pick is `PickUpgrade{offerId, choice}` on the control stream; the authority applies it at its next tick and reports the result to the owner as an event; it refuses a pick whose offer id is not an open offer to that player, a choice outside the offer, or a second pick of one offer.

It counts a malformed pick (an offer id it never issued, a choice out of range) like a forged command, and a stale or repeated one (a double click, or a pick in flight when the offer closed) apart, so honest races are not counted with cheats.

Track state (levels and picks per unit type and per weapon type) is owner class and is sent to the owner when it changes; owner is the starting class, and who else sees picks is ADR 0005's OQ-0005-AB15 (GD-PICK-VIS, Mustafa's); what a pick changes inside the prediction scope reaches the owner in the own-state section (part 4).
A purchase is `Buy{unitId}` on the control stream, for a unit or a vehicle ("the purchase names a unit, never a weapon":

ADR 0005 AB-8's table); the authority applies it at its next tick only if the id exists in the mode's content, the team has reached its tier (ADR 0005 AB-5), the player can pay the price (personal money, LOOP_V2 §3, power-plant pricing included) and stands at the team's own buy terminal (LOOP_V2 §2, §5), these conditions being rule data (ADR 0005 AB-5); it reports the result to the owner as an event, counts refusals as it counts picks, and never predicts a purchase.

A pickup is asked for through the command's existing button edges, with no message of its own; which act a press means where a pickup lies within reach of an uplink or a cache (a steal is holding E, LOOP_V2 §4 step 4; picking up and placing a cache, steps 2 and 3, name no key) is rule data (ADR 0005, OQ-0005-AB9's list).

The authority picks the pickup from its own state, so a command can never name a pickup into existence, and it refuses one it did not place, one already taken, or one outside the pickup rule (rule data:
Neither offers, picks, purchases nor pickups are predicted (pickups interim:

*Why:* the tracks belong to the player, so they are owner data the server holds, and offers that are never predicted need no client copy of the random stream that draws them (its kind is ADR 0004's); a purchase changes money, the authority's alone.
*Research:* no research id concerns upgrades; the parts used are R2-INT-REC5's classes, R2-SYNC-REC2's validation and R2-SYNC-F17 (Quake III's predicted pickups, the alternative OQ-0001-10 weighs);
R2's estimate already counts buys among the reliable gameplay events (r2-netcode.md, worked bandwidth estimate, line 1760).
*Need:* UPGRADE-SCOPE; purchases:
VISION_V2 §6.5 (the economy server-side).

Upgrade offers, pick and purchase results, track changes, hit confirmations, kills and drops are not separate message types: they are gameplay events or owner-section fields inside `Snapshot`, each with its class.

The estimate is R2's own scene, not the stress scene (GLOSSARY.md:415–416): the proof test's load fires 700 shots a second (R2-SYNC-REC5 mark 4), which alone adds (700 − 72) × 4 B × 8 ≈ 20.1 kbps (R2's shot events:

1.5 per player per second at 4 B, r2-netcode.md line 1759, so 72 a second at N = 48; arithmetic), so the 160 kbps mean is judged in R2's estimate scene and the stress scene is held by the cap (the budgets table).

- **Upstream per client:** R2's estimate assumes 8 B commands, newest plus 3 repeats: about 22.3 kbps at 30 sends per second (option U1's 44.6 kbps at 60 sends per second, halved; r2-netcode.md, Options, Brief question 2, table C, lines 1704–1710).

Part 5's command is larger: its aim point alone is up to 80 bits, beside the tick, sequence, move vector, buttons, press counters and view time, about 15–20 B in all (the perf review's estimate, 2026-11-02; the real size is measured, R2-XU-OQ4).
With the newest-received acknowledgement (part 5), a datagram carries the commands of one round trip plus up to two ticks of waiting (the snapshot's and the client's):
80–186.7 ms at P2's 100 ± 20 ms, so 3 to 6 commands ((80 to 186.7) ÷ 33.3, rounded up; arithmetic).

Sent whole (U1), with a header of about 6 B (an assumption) and the 57 B of IPv4 transport overhead (r2-netcode.md, line 1742), at 30 datagrams a second (240 bits a second per byte of datagram), that is (3 × 15 + 63) × 240 ≈ 25.9 to (6 × 20 + 63) × 240 ≈ 43.9 kbps at P2, and at the cap of 8, reached at P3 and P4 or after a loss, (8 × 15 + 63) × 240 ≈ 43.9 to (8 × 20 + 63) × 240 ≈ 53.5 kbps, against a mark of at most 48 kbps (IPv4:
R2-BUD-REC1), 200 B per datagram (48,000 ÷ 8 ÷ 30).
